content: The Sino-implant, a long-acting subdermal contraceptive implant that releases levonorgestrel, has been studied extensively. Research from 1993 highlighted its effectiveness during the first year of use. A systematic review in 2010 evaluated randomized controlled trials of the Sino-implant (II), confirming its efficacy and safety profile. The World Health Organization (WHO) published the fifth edition of its Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use in 2015, providing comprehensive guidelines for contraceptive methods, including subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA-SC). This formulation, containing 104 mg of DMPA, was introduced as a new option for progestogen-only injectables (POIs). Recommendations for initiating DMPA-SC align with those for other POIs, such as intramuscular DMPA (DMPA-IM) and norethisterone enanthate (NET-EN). Women can start DMPA-SC within seven days of the onset of menstrual bleeding or at any other time if pregnancy can be reasonably excluded. Additional guidance is provided for postpartum, post-abortion, amenorrheic women, and those switching from other contraceptive methods. Although no direct evidence exists regarding the timing of DMPA-SC initiation, recommendations are based on indirect evidence from studies on DMPA-IM. The pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, safety profiles, and mechanisms of action of DMPA-SC and DMPA-IM are similar, allowing extrapolation of data. Studies have shown that both formulations demonstrate comparable contraceptive efficacy and effects on serum estradiol levels. The WHO's guideline development group (GDG) reviewed evidence from systematic reviews and concluded that DMPA-SC can be safely initiated under the same conditions as DMPA-IM. Routine laboratory tests, pelvic/genital examinations, and cervical cancer screening are not necessary for determining eligibility for DMPA-SC use. These recommendations aim to reduce barriers to contraceptive access while maintaining safety and efficacy. For reinjection intervals, DMPA-SC should be administered every three months. Evidence suggests that reinjections can be given up to four weeks late without compromising contraceptive protection, but this should not extend the regular interval. Delayed reinjections may increase the risk of unintended pregnancy. The GDG classified these recommendations as strong, despite the very low quality of direct evidence, due to the significant benefits of preventing unintended pregnancies. The GDG also reviewed evidence on the combined contraceptive transdermal patch and vaginal ring. Recommendations for initiating these methods are consistent with those for combined oral contraceptives (COCs). Women can start these methods within five days of menstrual bleeding or at any other time if pregnancy can be excluded. Evidence suggests no differences in pregnancy rates or side effects based on the timing of initiation. The GDG emphasized the importance of facilitating access to these methods while ensuring safety and efficacy. In summary, the recommendations for DMPA-SC, the patch, and the vaginal ring are based on a combination of direct and indirect evidence, prioritizing women's safety, preferences, and access to effective contraception.
